title: How to cook unpolished rice: soaking, ratios and methods
summary: Cook unpolished rice soft and fluffy: how long to soak, water ratios for pot, pressure cooker and rice cooker, and fixes for hard or mushy rice.
body:
Unpolished rice still has its bran, the thin brown or red layer that polishing removes from white rice. That layer is what makes it nutty and chewy, and it also slows down water getting into the grain. Cook it like white rice and you'll get grains that are hard in the middle. The fix is simple: soak it, give it more water, and give it more time.

## Before you start: rinse and soak

**Rinse** the rice in a bowl of water, swirling it with your hand, then pour the water off. Do this 2–3 times, until the water is only slightly cloudy. It washes off dust and loose starch.

**Soak** it in plenty of cold water:

- 30 minutes is enough for everyday cooking and makes the biggest difference.
- 1–2 hours gives softer, more even grains.
- Overnight (up to about 8 hours) gives the softest result. Keep it in the fridge in hot weather.

The longer you soak, the less water and time the rice needs. Drain it well before cooking.

## How much rice and water

A standard 240 ml cup holds about 180–200 g of uncooked rice. Allow roughly 70–80 g of uncooked rice per person for a main meal; it about triples in volume once cooked.

These ratios are by volume, for rice soaked about 30 minutes. Use the lower end for longer soaks or slender grains, the higher end for bolder grains or if you like it soft.

- **Stovetop (absorption)**: 1 cup rice to 2–2½ cups water.
- **Pressure cooker**: 1 cup rice to 2–2¼ cups water.
- **Rice cooker**: follow the "brown rice" line or setting.
- **Pasta method**: 1 cup rice to 6–8 cups water, drained at the end.

## Method 1: Stovetop

- Put the drained rice, water and a pinch of salt in a heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid.
- Bring it to a boil, then turn the heat to its lowest setting and cover.
- Simmer for 30–45 minutes without lifting the lid too often. Start checking at 30.
- When the water has been absorbed and the grains are tender, take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes.
- Fluff it gently with a fork.

## Method 2: Pressure cooker

The pressure cooker is how most Indian kitchens cook unpolished rice, and it is the fastest way.

- Add the drained rice, water and salt to the cooker.
- Close it and cook on medium heat for about 3–4 whistles, or about 10–12 minutes at full pressure in an electric pressure cooker.
- Turn off the heat and let the pressure drop by itself before you open it. The rice keeps cooking as it rests.

If your rice comes out too firm, add a quarter cup of water next time or one more whistle. If it is too soft, do the opposite.

## Method 3: Rice cooker

Use the "brown rice" setting if your cooker has one; it soaks and cooks for longer than the white rice setting. If it doesn't, soak the rice first for at least an hour and add an extra quarter cup of water per cup of rice. Leave it on "keep warm" for 10 minutes after it switches off.

## Method 4: The pasta (draining) method

This is the most forgiving method and gives separate, non-sticky grains, which suits pulao, fried rice and rice salads.

- Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it.
- Add the soaked rice and boil it uncovered for 25–35 minutes, stirring now and then.
- Taste a grain. When it is tender, drain it in a colander.
- Return it to the pot, cover, and let it steam off the heat for 10 minutes.

## Troubleshooting

- **Hard in the middle**: it needed more soaking, water or time. Sprinkle in 2–3 tablespoons of hot water, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for another 5–10 minutes.
- **Mushy or sticky**: too much water or too long a soak. Use less water next time, rinse more thoroughly, or try the pasta method.
- **Burnt at the bottom**: the heat was too high or the pot too thin. Use a heavy pot, the lowest flame, or a flat tawa (griddle) under the pot.
- **Some grains cooked, some hard**: the rice wasn't soaked evenly or was stirred during absorption cooking. Soak in plenty of water and leave the lid on.
- **Smells stale or sour**: the rice itself is old. Unpolished rice keeps for less time than white rice, because its bran contains oil.

## Storing unpolished rice

- **Uncooked**: in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Buy amounts you'll use within a few months, and in a hot, humid kitchen keep it in the fridge. Use it before the best-before date on the pack.
- **Cooked**: cool it quickly, refrigerate within an hour, and eat it within a day. Reheat it until it is steaming hot all the way through.

Our Karjat 3, Kolam rice from Wada and Red Rice are milled in a single pass only to remove the husk, so the bran and germ stay on and the methods above all apply. Read [red rice vs brown rice vs white rice](/learn/red-rice-vs-brown-rice-vs-white-rice/) to compare them.
